artworks.title: Ino, Queen of Thebes (Leucothea)
artworks.description: Rayol's white marble for the Bosquet des Dômes at Versailles shows Ino transformed into the sea-goddess Leucothea, receiving sailors' offerings. Cadmus' daughter who leapt with Melicertes rises here as protectress of those who sail — Theban queen remade as white goddess of the surf.

artworks.title: Odysseus and Ino
artworks.description: Allori paints the Odyssey's sea rescue: Ino-Leucothea offers Odysseus her immortal veil as he struggles in the waves after leaving Calypso. The Theban queen-turned-goddess becomes the hand that saves the nostos.

artworks.title: Athamas Killing the Son of Ino
artworks.description: Gandolfi's canvas stages the madness Hera sends upon Athamas: he turns on Ino's children as she flees toward the cliff. The painting holds Ino at the instant before the leap that will make her Leucothea — stepmother, victim, and soon a goddess of the sea.

artworks.title: Leucothea Rescuing Ulysses
artworks.description: Bannister's American landscape-toned myth shows Leucothea — Ino deified — coming to Odysseus in the storm. The White Goddess of sailors is painted as a presence of rescue rather than court allegory, the Theban leap fulfilled as mercy on the open sea.

artworks.title: Ino and Melicertes
artworks.description: Granier's marble group for the demi-lune of Apollo's Basin at Versailles shows Ino with Melicertes at the moment of their sea-change. Mother and child become Leucothea and Palaemon — the Theban flight cast in stone for Louis XIV's gardens.

popCulture.title: Leucothea
popCulture.description: Ino's afterlife is the white sea-goddess Leucothea — the Theban queen who leaps with Melicertes and rises to save drowning Odysseus.

popCulture.title: Ino (Greek mythology)
popCulture.description: Ino remains Cadmus' daughter who nursed Dionysus and fled Athamas' madness — stepmother, victim, and finally a goddess of the surf.
